title: Families of Organic Compounds: Reading Functional Groups

info.text: Organic compounds come in families defined by small, characteristic groups: hydrocarbon frameworks (alkane, alkene, alkyne, arene), single-bond heteroatom families (alkyl halide, alcohol, ether, amine, thiol), the carbonyl core and its acid-derived relatives (carboxylic acid, ester, amide, acid chloride), and the carbon–nitrogen multiple bonds (nitrile, imine) — with R groups abstracting the framework and heteroatoms naming most families.

citations.title: 3.1: Functional Groups — Organic Chemistry (Morsch et al.)
citations.author: Steven Farmer, Dietmar Kennepohl, Layne Morsch, Krista Cunningham, Tim Soderberg

clusters.name: Hydrocarbon frameworks
clusters.fact: A skeleton of only carbon and hydrogen is classified by its bonding: all single bonds is an alkane (saturated — full of hydrogen), a C=C double bond is an alkene, a C≡C triple bond is an alkyne, and a planar aromatic ring is an arene.

termInfo.alkane: Only single bonds, to carbon and hydrogen — saturated, meaning every carbon carries the maximum possible hydrogen. Methane and octane are the everyday examples.
termInfo.alkene: A carbon–carbon double bond; the alkene carbons are trigonal planar (sp²), and the bond's rigidity can give cis and trans forms.
termInfo.alkyne: A carbon–carbon triple bond; linear geometry at the sp carbons. Ethyne (acetylene) feeds welding torches.
termInfo.arene: A planar aromatic ring such as benzene or naphthalene — its own classification, beyond the saturated/unsaturated split.

clusters.name: Single-bond heteroatom families
clusters.fact: Put one heteroatom into a saturated framework through single bonds and a family appears: carbon–halogen is an alkyl halide, carbon–OH is an alcohol, oxygen between two carbons is an ether, carbon–nitrogen is an amine, and the sulfur analog of an alcohol is a thiol.

termInfo.alkyl halide: An alkane carbon bonded to a halogen (F, Cl, Br, I — often written X). Common in the laboratory, quite rare in biomolecules.
termInfo.alcohol: A carbon single-bonded to an OH (a hydroxyl); how many other carbons that carbon touches makes the alcohol primary, secondary, or tertiary.
termInfo.ether: An oxygen bonded to two carbons — diethyl ether was one of the first anesthetics and remains a common laboratory solvent.
termInfo.amine: Nitrogen with single bonds to hydrogens and carbons; amines are basic and readily protonated to ammonium ions.
termInfo.thiol: The sulfur analog of an alcohol: an SH where the alcohol's OH sits (the prefix thio- refers to sulfur).

clusters.name: The carbonyl core
clusters.fact: The carbon–oxygen double bond is the carbonyl; when its carbon sees only carbons and hydrogen it makes the two closely related, similarly reacting families: ketones (two carbon neighbors) and aldehydes (one hydrogen neighbor — formaldehyde the exception with two).

termInfo.ketone: A carbonyl whose carbon bonds to two other carbons — acetone is the everyday example.
termInfo.aldehyde: A carbonyl whose carbon bonds to one hydrogen and one carbon (formaldehyde is the exception, with two hydrogens).

clusters.name: Carboxylic acid derivatives
clusters.fact: When a carbonyl carbon bonds to a heteroatom instead of only C/H, the group joins the carboxylic acid derivative family: OH gives the carboxylic acid (readily deprotonated to a carboxylate), O–C gives an ester, N gives an amide, Cl gives an acid chloride.

termInfo.carboxylic acid: A carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl; acidic, meaning it readily loses that proton to become a carboxylate. Acetic acid is the vinegar member.
termInfo.ester: A carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is itself bonded to another carbon — readable as a carbonyl plus an alcohol.
termInfo.amide: A carbonyl bonded to a nitrogen bearing hydrogens, carbons, or both — readable as a carbonyl plus an amine.
termInfo.acid chloride: A carbonyl bonded to a chlorine — the table's acid halide, e.g. ethanoyl (acetyl) chloride.

clusters.name: Nitrogen multiple-bond families
clusters.fact: Carbon–nitrogen multiple bonds outside the carbonyl framework form their own families: the C≡N triple bond is a nitrile (cyano group), and the C=N double bond is an imine.

termInfo.nitrile: A carbon triple-bonded to a nitrogen, often called a cyano group; the tables file it under multiple bonds to heteroatoms.
termInfo.imine: A carbon–nitrogen double bond — sometimes called a Schiff base.

clusters.name: The functional-group lens
clusters.fact: A functional group is a small group of atoms with characteristic reactivity — the same behavior shows up wherever the group occurs; the rest of the molecule is abstracted as an R group, and heteroatom names the non-carbon, non-hydrogen atoms that define most families.

termInfo.functional group: A small group of atoms with characteristic reactivity — a particular group almost always displays its distinctive chemical behavior in any compound that carries it.
termInfo.R group: The abbreviation for the part of the molecule outside the region of interest — read it as 'any carbon framework here'.
termInfo.heteroatom: In organic chemistry, any atom other than carbon or hydrogen — oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, or a halogen — whose identity names most of the single-bond families.

bridges.term: the framework is the R group
bridges.fact: The hydrocarbon framework is what R abbreviates — the part of the molecule outside the group of interest; alkanes themselves are the simplest functional group, the one listings tend to ignore.
bridges.info: When a formula shows R, read 'any carbon framework here'.

bridges.fact: One look at which non-carbon atom carries the single bonds names the family: a halogen gives an alkyl halide, OH gives an alcohol, O between two carbons an ether, N an amine, S a thiol.
The carbonyl world splits by what sits next to the C=O carbon: only carbons and hydrogen gives aldehydes and ketones; a heteroatom on the other side makes it a carboxylic acid derivative.
bridges.info: First question at any C=O: are both neighbors C/H, or is one a heteroatom?

bridges.fact: Each single-bond family is an alkane framework with one substitution: a halogen where an H was makes an alkyl halide, an OH makes an alcohol, nitrogen makes an amine — the parent shows through.
Swap a carbonyl oxygen for nitrogen and the other multiple-bond families appear: C=O becomes C=N (an imine), and the triple-bond C≡N is a nitrile.
An ester is a carbonyl bonded to an alcohol and an amide is a carbonyl bonded to an amine — spot an acid derivative by seeing which single-bond family hangs off the carbonyl carbon.
Real compounds wear several families at once: glucose is an aldehyde with five alcohol groups, fructose a ketone with five alcohols — recognition is per group, not per molecule.
bridges.info: Aspirin: an arene plus a carboxylic acid plus an ester — three families, one molecule.

lenses.prompt: Which two hydrocarbon families does the classification call unsaturated — carrying fewer hydrogens than the saturated maximum?
lenses.explanation: Alkanes are saturated: every carbon carries its maximum hydrogen. The double- and triple-bonded carbons of alkenes and alkynes hold fewer hydrogens, hence unsaturated. Arenes are filed as their own planar-ring family rather than in this split.

lenses.prompt: Two families on this board carry an O–H — which are they?
lenses.explanation: The alcohol's OH hangs from a saturated carbon; the carboxylic acid's OH hangs from the carbonyl carbon — same bond, different carbon, which is why the acid readily loses that proton. The ether's oxygen bonds two carbons and no hydrogen at all.

lenses.prompt: Which family's carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen?
lenses.explanation: Aldehydes carry exactly one hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon (formaldehyde carries two); ketones carry only carbons, and the acid derivatives carry a heteroatom instead.

lenses.prompt: Which two members of the acid-derivative family bond an oxygen to the carbonyl carbon?
lenses.explanation: The acid's oxygen is the OH; the ester's is an O that continues on to another carbon. The amide's neighbor is nitrogen and the acid chloride's is chlorine — which is exactly how you tell all four apart.

lenses.prompt: Sweep the board: which families put nitrogen into the molecule?
lenses.explanation: Four different ways for one element to enter: single-bonded N is an amine; N sitting on a carbonyl carbon is an amide; a C≡N triple bond is a nitrile; a C=N double bond is an imine. Every O, S, and halogen family stays out.

lenses.prompt: Which two of these name a multi-atom part of a molecule rather than a single atom?
lenses.explanation: The functional group is the reactive atom-group and the R group is the abstracted framework it rides on — both are multi-atom parts. Heteroatom is the one atom-level word, and it does the family-naming work.

entries.reason: Play after naming the families: the next lesson classifies same-formula pairs — including the cis–trans alkene pairs met here — by the mirror test.

learningIntroduction.title: Learning organic chemistry by families
learningIntroduction.summary: Why small atom-groups, not whole molecules, are the units of organic chemistry.

content.text:
Why can a chemist glance at a structure and say 'ester' in a second? Because organic chemistry is learned by families: small groups of atoms — a double bond here, an OH there, a carbonyl with a heteroatom neighbor — bring the same characteristic behavior wherever they appear, whether the molecule is a painkiller, a banana's ripening signal, or a hormone. Reading a structure fluently means spotting those groups: first the carbon framework, then the heteroatoms bonded through single bonds, then the carbonyls and whatever hangs off them.

The objective: given any simple organic structure, name its family or families — and know why that naming matters. Each family name is a promise about behavior: carboxylic acids give up a proton, amines accept one, double and triple bonds add hydrogen, and ester linkages hold fats and flavors together. Recognition first; behavior follows.
